The “continental” Apennines

We shall call “continental” Apennines the first stretch of our route, that is, the one within which all watercourses flow into the Po river basin, reaching the plain and emptying into the Adriatic Sea. The “maritime” Apennines, by contrast, are those whose watercourses flow – directly or as tributaries of other rivers or torrents – into the Ligurian Sea.

Salt and salt springs

Geologically, the relief along whose ridge the Via del Cifalco runs “originates” at the confluence of the Trebbia and the Aveto. It is curious that this Salt Road should begin (or end, depending on one’s point of view) precisely in a place where there is a salt spring.

Geologically, this phenomenon is due to groundwater passing through deep rock formations, which preserve what remains of ancient evaporite basins or other underground saline circulations that are common in the tectonic and clay units of the Apennines.

In the Middle Ages, the local people already exploited this source, one of many in Val d’Aveto (the very place name Salsominore, a little further upstream, confirms it). In the 12th century, the Comune of Piacenza, having seized the main estates of the upper Val Trebbia, also took possession of the Cerignale salt spring, which later passed to the Doria family as well. Until the 1940s, the people of Cerignale went on using it. Over the centuries, various floods of the Aveto gradually buried the spring. To this day the works are still buried, so much so that not even their exact location could be identified, were it not for the water that still wets the rock face, dark and dense, with an unmistakable brackish taste.

The realm of the beech wood

Our route begins a little upstream of the Trebbia-Aveto confluence, at Ponte Organasco, in Val Trebbia. Apart from the very first stretch of mixed woodland between Ponte Organasco, Cerignale and Oneto and then up to M. delle Tane, the distinctive feature of the Antica Via del Cifalco from the slopes of M. Dego to the watershed separating the “continental” from the “maritime” Apennines is undoubtedly the beech wood.

Beeches deserve the credit for shaping woods that are cool and pleasant in every season. Their leaves are an intense green in spring and summer, when they let the sunlight filter through and settle like molten gold on the undergrowth, and they take on autumn colours in the months of the foliage, before falling and withering in winter.

In the northern Apennines, they generally take over from oak and Turkey oak woods between 800 and 1000 metres of altitude, up to 1700/1800 m a.s.l. The beech was already present in Italy two million years ago, but it is only in the last 2500 years or so that it has prevailed in place of the silver fir, which disappeared because of climate change, extensive logging and also a structurally poor germination capacity. At Moglie (or Mogge) di Ertola, just below the pass of the same name, sub-fossil fir trunks have been found and have been the subject of specific studies, in particular by the Istituto Italiano di Storia e Protostoria.

Rocks and rocky environments

A glance at the Cifalco ridge makes it easy, even for those with little knowledge of the natural sciences, to tell reliefs – and peaks – of ophiolitic origin from sedimentary ones.

Ophiolitic rocks – from the Greek “ὄφις”, “snake”, because of the greenish patches scattered over the rocks – rise up like foreign bodies sprung from the bowels of the earth, and characterise the mountains with the most jagged outlines. Their shapes look wilder and more untamed precisely because they lack the evolutionary process that would have smoothed their roughness over time. They are extremely resistant to erosion and derive from submarine sub-effusive lava, a process that took place when these lands were covered by a single great ocean.

They come in different types depending on the conditions of solidification, which produced differences in colour, shape and texture. In the area between the Trebbia and the Aveto, the dominant ophiolites are serpentinites, peridotites and diabase. Typical examples of ophiolitic rocks along the Strada del Cifalco are the summit areas of M. Roccabruna (serpentinite) and M. Gifarco (diabase), but also the cluster of boulders that forms M. Castello del Fante (diabase).

The reliefs surrounding the ophiolites, on the other hand, are made of sedimentary rocks, that is, rocks formed over millennia by the accumulation and layering of organic and inorganic material deposited on the floor of that same ocean. Being more prone to erosion, they are lower than the “volcanic” ophiolitic rocks. They too fall into various families – mainly clay shales, limestones and sandstones. The latter, in particular, are widespread on the maritime watershed running along M. Caucaso and are the youngest of the group, formed from sandy sediments and debris of mountain ranges in the making. Shales, by contrast, are the oldest and therefore those most worn by the weather: such is the case, for example, of the rocks of the Passo della Scoglina, at the foot of M. Caucaso.

If the rocks least subject to erosion are ophiolites, limestones and sandstones, then one need only look at the Cifalco range to get a rough idea of how they are distributed along it. The rivers and torrents that have carved the flanks of the massif on its two sides chose precisely the softest rocks to slide down to the valley. The Cifalco ridge is thus the backbone of a marvellous sculpture inlaid by water, wind and snow over countless centuries.

Fauna

Both in the beech woods and in the rocky habitats, the area of the Strada del Cifalco is far more frequented by animals than by human beings.

A vast – if often invisible – community of mammals lives in the beech woods of the Antica Via del Cifalco, including the yellow-necked mouse, the bank vole and the edible dormouse. Among birds, the wood warbler – though rare – is still present, along with the bullfinch, the song thrush and the mistle thrush.

The presence of mammals is also very rich: wild boar, roe deer, fallow deer, red deer, foxes, badgers and wolves, which have returned in force to the Apennines since the 1980s after decades of silence. Up to that same period, otters were documented in the torrents running down the Aveto side, but for 50 years now no sightings have been reported.

The rocky habitats are a paradise for birdlife, especially for birds of prey: peregrine falcon, short-toed eagle, goshawk, buzzard, kestrel, sparrowhawk and even the golden eagle, albeit very rare. On the most inhospitable slopes of the ophiolitic rocks, black redstarts, rock thrushes, wheatears, calandra larks and nightjars find an ideal habitat.

Grass snakes and vipers also frequent these slopes, taking advantage of the exposure to the sun that allows them – as ectothermic vertebrates – to reach the body temperature they need.

Around the wetlands, such as in particular the Lago della Nave, the alpine newt, the Italian crested newt and the smooth newt thrive.

From spring onwards the variety of butterflies is enormous, among which the magnificent – and very ancient – Parnassius Apollo deserves a mention, with its unmistakable pair of red spots on each of its two hind wings. It survived the last ice ages by migrating south and then, little by little, returning north.

The area between M. Roccabruna, M. Gifarco and the Lago della Nave is also designated a Site of Community Importance (SIC – reference no. IT1331012) and therefore subject to the special conservation measures of the Natura 2000 network, proof of the significant environmental value of that stretch of ridge. Protection is aimed in particular at safeguarding the beech woods, the mountain grasslands and endemic plant and animal species, such as in particular the alpine newt, the Italian crested newt and the smooth newt, which thrive in large numbers in the Lago della Nave.

The realm of the wolf

The question of the wolf deserves a more in-depth discussion. The first sightings in our Apennines since the period after the Second World War date back to 1983 on the Antola ridge, that is, the one opposite the Cifalco, on the other side of the Valtrebbia. The first attacks on livestock, on the other hand, were reported in Val Borbera in 1985, the year that also saw the first carcass found since the one in Val d’Aveto in 1946, long believed to be that of “the last” specimen.

The gradual return of the wolf has fired up public debate on these mountains. Tension has been rising over the last 10 years, when the number of wolves has indeed grown at a dizzying pace and attacks have become much more frequent, including on domestic dogs (not only hunting dogs). Today the issue is red-hot along the whole stretch of the Apennines between the Taro and the Scrivia (and beyond), to the point of being a key factor in the local elections of the mountain Comuni.

It is difficult to take a stand here on such a complex issue: on the one hand there is a key player for biodiversity, a majestic mammal and a symbol of history, local culture and nature of immeasurable social and aesthetic value; on the other, these already depopulated mountains are home to farmers, livestock breeders and other “holdouts”. Given the unfavourable conditions in which they work, they are not so well protected that they can be expected to shoulder, without a murmur, a further complication in their daily lives. Clearly a compromise solution is called for.

On this point, we shall merely draw attention to a few scientific and factual data:

  • The wolf never became entirely extinct in the Italian Apennines. It has therefore never been reintroduced, let alone deliberately crossed with other non-native species. Crosses with feral domestic dogs and Czechoslovakian wolfdogs have occurred, but never intentionally: indeed, it is hard to see what interest anyone would have had in such an operation.
  • From its historic population low, estimated by the WWF at 180-200 specimens in the whole of Italy in the early 1970s, its recovery has been accompanied by favourable legislation at international and European level, awareness campaigns, an increase in prey – including the explosion of wild boar and roe deer we have witnessed everywhere over the last two decades – and the great resilience and adaptability of the species.
  • To date, not a single case of one or more wolves attacking a human being has been recorded in Italy, unlike what has happened with wild boar and even with domestic dogs. There have recently been a few reports, but no attack has yet been proven.
  • Science is unanimous in regarding the wolf as the cost-benefit animal par excellence: it will therefore favour livestock and other mammals only when these are poorly guarded or when more traditional prey such as ungulates are present in abnormally low numbers, in particular because of poaching and habitat loss.

From the above, it seems in everyone’s interest to support, technically, logistically and financially, adequate containment measures and fair compensation procedures for operators who have suffered attacks. At present, in Italy, the former are wholly inadequate and the latter utterly ridiculous, both in the amounts paid out and in the paperwork involved. If you talk to the livestock breeders who live around the Via del Cifalco, they will tell you about their dismal experience with the competent authorities.

At the same time, we are witnessing a downgrading of the wolf’s level of legal protection, which strikes us as a “shortcut”. On the ground, meanwhile, a genuine extermination is under way, founded on the idea of taking the law into one’s own hands, which is not talked about enough in the mainstream press and indeed meets with the utter passivity of the competent authorities. Besides the usual firearms, the scattering of poisoned baits in the forest – so much for all the other animals that swallow them! – has become a vehicle of indiscriminate killing and of havoc in the ecosystems, and is sadly on a worrying rise.

Climate

The mountains of this area have historically had very high rainfall in every season. The meeting of the warm air coming from the coast with the colder air of the “continental” Apennine valleys is in fact the cause of frequent storms. Even in summer, it is not unusual to see menacing black clouds gather over the peaks, while the sky above, for those watching from the plain or from the sea, stays clear. Likewise, snowfall in the winter months has always been abundant. It is nonetheless evident – to anyone, except those who refuse to acknowledge it – that climate change is upsetting, and in part has already upset, these balances.

In any case, the closeness of the sea is also the cause of thick fogs that often form along the watershed. Overall sunshine is low and soil moisture is high even at the height of summer, when in the hottest hours of the day the heat can be scorching even on the ridge.

One of the most moving moments of the walk is when you pass from the last beech woods of M. Caucaso, where the humidity still fills your nostrils and you feel light years away from the sea, to the other side of the watershed, where on the contrary, all of a sudden, you breathe the Mediterranean.

The “maritime” Apennines

Nature on the south face of M. Caucaso

Crossing the watershed on the summit of M. Caucaso is therefore the most radical break of the whole route, both in terms of nature and of culture. It is highly recommended to linger on the majestic summit from which the sea can be admired, perhaps stopping at the beautiful summit refuge: this is perhaps the point where, for the first time, you realise how far you have come.

In May, when the south face of M. Caucaso is covered by a yellow carpet of flowering broom, this descent is unforgettable. The sea air begins to rise up the valleys, and the cool beech woods in which you have been immersed for days, and which still clothed the north face of the same mountain, already seem a distant memory. Here we are inside the Special Area of Conservation (ZSC) “Monte Caucaso” (reference no. IT1331811), which covers 293 hectares rich in botanical rarities, including a multitude of succulents, among which the very rare Mondovì stonecrop (Sedum monregalense) stands out. Moreover, thanks to the variety of its habitats, with rocky areas alongside grasslands, forests and watercourses, it is a particularly inviting environment for a rich birdlife and for other species that indicate habitat quality, such as the beetle Nebria tibialis tibialis.

Val Fontanabuona

Squeezed between the most glamorous coastal strip of the Tigullio on one side and the expanse of endless beech woods on the other, Val Fontanabuona has fallen victim to haphazard urban sprawl on the valley floor, especially around the Entella plain. This has considerably undervalued its otherwise unquestionably rich historical, landscape and cultural heritage. Those who discover it fall in love with it: a great many environmental guides work exclusively in this valley, proof of the endless range of options that can be offered to visitors!

Unlike most of the valleys in the region, which lie perpendicular to the coast, it runs lengthwise, parallel to the sea for about 35 kilometres behind the Promontorio di Portofino. This configuration creates a unique microclimate and biodiversity, partly protected by the Parco Naturale Regionale dell'Aveto.

Val Fontanabuona is the chestnut valley par excellence. In the lowest and warmest areas, transitional formations with Mediterranean scrub and olive groves hold out.

With Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto it shares the problem of the inexorable depopulation of its villages. Terraces, vegetable gardens, crumbling wayside shrines, abandoned houses: all of them are vestiges of a civilisation rejected and supplanted by that of prosperity (real or supposed). What the landscape of Val Fontanabuona tells us, as indeed in Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto too, is less the outcome of a succession of kings, lords and rulers than small episodes of humble daily life: pastures on grassy ridges with the characteristic “casoni” where livestock were sheltered, wooden crosses at the edges of meadows, little stone bridges, and many dry-stone walls, now largely destroyed.

The small valley of the Neirone torrent, which flows into the Lavagna near Gattorna, is also part of the Val Fontanabuona basin. The descent from the Caucaso, with its wide openings, plunges decisively into it when the path comes close to a double dry-stone wall. The scrub thickens: first ferns and then heather dominate a dense and often chaotic undergrowth, inside a chestnut wood mixed with other varieties, with the celebrated round beech that gives its name to the locality of the same name above Pian del Pero. From Neirone onwards, the path runs alongside the torrent of the same name, which forms inviting pools of cold but crystal-clear water. A pity that this clashes with the state of upkeep of the wood, which has become, in spite of itself, the “Valley of wonders” (see the section “The stages of the Via del Cifalco through history, nature and culture”, in the part devoted to Neirone and Gattorna). We hope one day to be able to give this wood back the future it deserves.

The Parco del M. di Portofino

Everything has been said and written about the Parco del M. di Portofino and the village of the same name. And yet those who visit it never cease to marvel at it, to become passionate about it, to want to know more.

It is first and foremost a wonder of geology. The summit of M. di Portofino rises above 600 metres, just one kilometre as the crow flies from the coast; its ridge, beneath which runs the very last stretch of the Strada del Cifalco on the route proposed here, slopes down towards a promontory that for a few hundred metres more still separates the Tigullio from the Golfo Paradiso and shelters the world-famous little harbour.

In terms of nature, it is one of the most interesting places in northern Italy and expresses a perfect union of sea and forest. The idea, ever-present on the Ligurian Levante, that the mountains plunge into the sea and there carry on undaunted in their race towards the abyss is expressed in every possible form on M. di Portofino.

A particular feature of the Parco del M. di Portofino is that it is covered by a largely “mesophilous” woodland, that is, one sharply divided between areas dried out by the heat and the dryness of the sea and others with very high levels of humidity.

This means that there are corners of “continental” nature just a few steps from the sea. Such is the case of the Niasca chestnut grove, between Portofino Mare and Paraggi. This little valley is deeply enclosed and gets very few hours of sun in the course of the day, which favours a high humidity that led the monks of the nearby hermitage to plant a chestnut grove there as early as the Middle Ages. It would seem the operation worked: although abandoned since the Second World War, chestnut trees still thrive today to within a few metres of the shore.

The chestnut groves live alongside diametrically opposed natural features, such as the widespread presence of ferns: those found in the Park today descend from ones dating back to the Devonian and the Carboniferous (from 395 to 286 million years ago, before the dinosaurs!). On the other hand, on the stretch along the Sella della Gaixella as far as Pietre Strette, the many alternations of chestnut groves, holm oak woods and hop hornbeam woods give way at once to the most classic Mediterranean scrub as soon as you go down one of the flanks of the saddle to reach the sea.

Nor should we overlook the signs of man’s patient work in adapting the land to his needs, over long centuries in which the constructive and destructive sides of the human footprint still found an acceptable balance. The terraces supported by dry-stone walls and planted with olives, capers and lemons become more and more frequent from Ruta onwards, especially for those going down to San Rocco and Camogli.

This diversity gives rise to complex ecosystems, with a varied biodiversity and an ever-changing landscape, which makes the ride from Ruta onwards an unceasing parade of different environments, scents and scenery.

Arriving near the sea, and therefore at the Golfo Paradiso – on the Camogli side – and at the Tigullio – on the Portofino side – coincides with a drastic change in the flora.

The cliffs of the Ligurian Levante remain rich in adaptable species, since they can live in highly saline environments. Yet they are also fragile, threatened as they are by pollution, climate change and urbanisation. This is the case not only of the famous rock samphire, but also of the sea daffodil, the sea holly and the yellow horned poppy, common along the railway lines that run close to the water. Conifers – maritime pine, stone pine and Aleppo pine – complete the wooded landscape together with the holm oak woods.

The coast of M. di Portofino, which juts out forcing sailors to cover more than double the 6.5 kilometres that as the crow flies would separate the castle of Camogli from that of Rapallo, is extremely stern where it meets the sea. Its southern slopes of conglomerate, a geologically young sedimentary rock and therefore resistant to erosion, allow these places to keep a forbidding and wild appearance even in the fine season, despite the hundreds of thousands of people who come to visit every year from the four corners of the globe.

Another wonder of Portofino and its surroundings is their state of conservation. Of course, the heavy traffic into the marinas means they are hardly remote places. Yet, given the ravaging of the landscape that has devastated the whole of Italy, particularly along the coasts, the state of preservation of the Park’s nature is little short of miraculous. The other villages of the Tigullio were unable to withstand the same pressure, starting with Rapallo, which has indeed become the archetype, in the Italian language, of that process of “rapallizzazione” that massacred it right up to the foot of the mountains.

None of this happens in Portofino, which owes a great deal to the establishment – in 1935 – of the Ente autonomo del M. di Portofino, which in 1978 became the Ente del Parco Naturale Regionale del M. di Portofino. And today some people are even talking about turning it into a National Park…

Whatever the criticisms levelled at it since its foundation, the Ente certainly has the historic merit of having always blocked the plan for a coastal road between Camogli and Portofino, which has been under discussion since the 1930s. For once, the army of property speculators who have ravished the Italian Peninsula far and wide had to lay down their arms.
